Experiment proposal.description: Papers related to Sherry's proposal on helping designers and PMs plan, communicate and interpret AI-assisted product experiments (matched 16 Oct 2026).

2309.10947.why: Your Gu et al. anchor: a design probe for how analysts check AI-generated analyses, which your designers would need without the coding background.

2309.10108.why: The "analysts responding to AI assistance" paper in your table; it covers AI help with analysis *planning*, which is close to your RQ1.

2504.13903.why: Experience doesn't change adoption but does change the mental model of AI's role.

2603.14225.why: Even experts skim agent output; relevant to your AI layer that opens PRs.

2502.08554.why: Explanations raise reliance even when the answer is wrong. Directly relevant to your AI-written hypotheses and captions.

2602.11567.why: Plants misinformation and measures who catches it, the same method as your "planted trap" evaluation.

2403.16812.why: Gets people to engage with an AI suggestion dimension by dimension instead of accepting or rejecting it whole.

2603.18895.why: A metric taxonomy (reliance, safety signals) you could borrow for the evaluation.

2603.08849.why: When the AI is available changes the quality of reasoning; relevant to your three-minute comprehension test.

2502.10526.why: The closest analogue to RQ1: it makes a technical specification (what to predict, when, for whom) readable and critiquable by non-data-scientists.

2402.15350.why: An in-situ pre-mortem while prototyping, with LLM-generated, editable harms. A direct precedent for your risk cards.

2309.09495.why: Shows the AI's understanding back to the user in plain language so they can correct it, like your editable inferred hypothesis.

2412.10999.why: An editable shared plan where steps are assigned to the human or the agent.

2502.01390.why: Human review of an AI plan before execution, and how that review affects trust.

2603.11677.why: Argues for showing consequences before acting, the same reasoning behind your duration slider and risk cards.

2510.14591.why: Infers the user's goal from behaviour and steers the AI with it, comparable to inferring the hypothesis from a code diff.

2603.29890.why: AI in PM concept testing: agents match the population distribution but miss on individuals. Useful caution on AI-inferred user intent.

2310.04329.why: Lets non-programmers specify something executable, a pattern for designers specifying instrumentation.

2604.16323.why: Argues that code diffs alone don't convey intent; relevant to inferring a hypothesis from a diff.

2504.15549.why: Step-by-step guided interaction beat full automation on control and learnability across data-analysis and visual-design tasks.

2402.15605.why: Measures whether the audience sees what the author intended, a method for your restatement-accuracy measure.

2601.11072.why: Plain text labels communicated worst and visual timelines communicated better. Relevant to how you label AI-generated captions.

2602.01796.why: A Figma tool that frames design feedback from UX, PM and engineering roles, the same cross-functional gap your brief bridges.

2403.13139.why: An LLM reading a design artifact and producing judgments designers act on.

2309.15237.why: Background on your population: designers keep agency and see AI as assistive.

2603.05848.why: Designers negotiate rigor and responsibility at team level, which supports "know when to call an analyst."

2401.14484.why: Established principles to position your own design principles against.

2401.08876.why: A pre-registered test of uncertainty displays: whether they help depends on task difficulty.

2603.22766.why: An uncertainty visualization that helps non-experts decide under many variables, similar to segments and guardrails.

2503.16114.why: Showing variability reduces undue trust but adds load, which is your "misreading drops without readers giving up" trade-off.

2405.20434.why: Compares ways of communicating how reliable AI text is, applicable to your AI-labelled captions.

2602.09631.why: A theory of what interaction asks of chart readers, useful for framing readers without statistics.

2310.01935.why: How professionals design charts for lay audiences.

2411.12299.why: Lay readers' heuristics versus statistical rationality when reading charts.

2502.11919.why: LLM-written natural-language analysis of a recommendation improves appropriate reliance, which bears on your caption-only role for the model.

2309.15723.why: A survey of AI tools that turn data into narrative, the space your results view sits in.

2403.09121.why: Turns analysis code into a communicable story, a step comparable to your results-to-design-judgment step.
